title: Shopping — and the form that appears when something isn't there
goal: Haggle, ask for quantities, and pay at the market — while setting up the genitive, the case with the most jobs: possession, negation, quantities, and a whole row of prepositions you use every day.
bekal: ask prices, ask for quantities, and understand your change
form the genitive singular and plural for all three noun genders
use the genitive after *nema*, after quantities, and after *iz, od, do, bez, kod*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Na pijaci Markale
dialogs.intro: Saturday morning at the Markale open-air market, in the city center. The wooden stalls are piled with vegetables, and every seller calls out to buyers with a nickname.

lines.id: Come on, young man! What would you like?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: How much is a kilo of apples?

lines.speaker: Prodavačica:
lines.text: Dvije marke i pedeset. Jako su dobre.

notes: **Count how many times a genitive ending shows up in this dialogue: *jabuka, kilograma, paradajza, krastavaca, sira, komšinice, maraka, feninga, kusura, Turske, Indonezije, posla*.** Twelve times in thirteen lines. That's why the genitive is called the busiest case in Bosnian — and why it comes this early.

***Nemam paradajza*, not *nemam paradajz*.** Negation pulls the noun into the genitive. *Imam vremena* and *nemam vremena* (I have / don't have time), *Ima kafe* and *nema kafe*. This rule also explains *nema problema* — a phrase you've been using since unit 4 without knowing why it ends in *-a*.

***Dajte mi* — "give me".** That's the polite command form of *dati*, plus *mi*, meaning "to me". The casual form is *Daj mi*. The little word *mi* is a dative form, set up in unit 13; for now learn *dajte mi* and *daj mi* as chunks — you'll use them in every shop.

***Kod* means "at (someone's place)".** *Kod komšinice* = at the neighbor's stall; *kod kuće* = at home; *kod doktora* = at the doctor's; *kod mene* = at my place. It works like French *chez*, and it's used all the time — once you recognize it, many sentences suddenly open up.

**Markale.** An open-air market in the heart of Sarajevo, and a heavy name in the city's history: it was shelled twice during the siege of 1992-1995. Today it's back to what it always was — a place where people argue over the price of tomatoes from seven in the morning. If you go, go early; after midday the best is gone.

grammars.title: Genitiv — the forms
body: The second case, and the most used of all seven. Its endings are few and regular; what takes time is recognizing when it's used — that's the second part.
after: **The easiest to remember: masculine and neuter words end in *-a* in the genitive singular.** *Grad → grada*, *pivo → piva*, *posao → posla*, *sir → sira*. One ending for two genders.

**The genitive plural of feminine and neuter words has no ending at all** — and that's exactly why it often looks like some other form. *Jabuke → jabuka*, *marke → maraka*, *piva → piva*. Note *maraka*: when dropping the ending would leave two consonants that are hard to say (*mark*), Bosnian slips an **-a-** into the middle. Likewise *sestra → sestara*, *djevojka → djevojaka*, *student → studenata*.

**The masculine genitive plural uses *-ova* or *-eva***, the same insert you know from the plural in unit 5: *grad → gradovi → gradova*, *nož → noževi → noževa*. Longer words just use *-a*: *studenti → studenata*, *prozori → prozora*.

**Adjectives follow, as usual:** *dobrog grada* (m/n singular), *dobre kafe* (f singular), *dobrih gradova* (plural, all genders). That plural ending *-ih* is the same for all three genders — one thing that's easier than it looks.

grammars.title: The five jobs of the genitive
body: This is the part that really takes time. All five often appear in the same sentence, so once you recognize the pattern, half of Bosnian becomes readable.

head: Job
Example
Meaning
rows: my brother's house, the city center
There's no coffee. I don't have time.
a kilo of apples, a glass of water, a little cheese, lots of people
*iz, od, do, bez, kod, poslije, prije, blizu, oko, zbog*
from, from, until, without, at, after, before, near, around, because of

after: **Possession: the same order as English "of".** *Kuća mog brata* = "the house of my brother" — the thing owned first, the owner after. There's no *'s*; instead the owner's ending changes: *brat → brata*, *Amina → Amine*, *grad → grada*.

**The prepositions you'll use most, all with the genitive:** *iz* (from, origin), *od* (from, since; also "than"), *do* (until, up to), *bez* (without), *kod* (at someone's place), *poslije* (after), *prije* (before), *blizu* (near), *pored* (next to), *oko* (around), *zbog* (because of), *umjesto* (instead of), *preko* (across, via).

**Quantity words are worth learning whole with their partners:** *malo* (a little), *puno / mnogo* (a lot), *dosta* (enough; also "quite a lot"), *nekoliko* (several), *pola* (half), *komad* (a piece), *čaša* (a glass), *flaša* (a bottle), *kilogram*, *litar*. All of them pull the next noun into the genitive — and if it's countable, into the genitive **plural**: *puno ljudi*, *nekoliko maraka*.

**One idea that ties it all together.** If you look closely, all five jobs circle around one notion: **part of**, **coming from**, or **none of**. The genitive is the case that points toward origin and parts — much like English "of" and "from". If you're unsure mid-sentence, ask yourself: is this about a portion, an origin, or an absence? If yes, it's almost certainly the genitive.

sections.title: Kupovina — shopping at the market and in shops

blocks.text: Bosnia has two different shopping worlds: the *pijaca* (open-air market, prices can be rounded, the seller remembers your face) and the *market* or *prodavnica* (supermarket, fixed prices). The sentences below work in both.

head: Bosanski
Say it
English
rows: Could you make it a bit cheaper?

blocks.title: Haggling: yes, but not everywhere
items: At the *pijaca*, rounding the price down is normal and not considered rude — especially if you're buying a lot or come near closing time. The phrase: *Može li malo jeftinije?* or simply *Hajde, za pet maraka?*
In supermarkets, pharmacies, and shops with price tags, nobody haggles at all. There, a different question is useful: *Imate li nešto jeftinije?* — do you have anything cheaper?

One habit worth copying: greet the seller first. A *Dobar dan!* before asking the price changes the whole tone of the conversation, and at a small market it often ends with a free piece of fruit to taste.
